Heat them up to scrape them easier Some of them have the foundation in with comb and we don't want to melt that But some of them do not and we could just fully heat those up
turns.response_html:
Heat is definitely the right path when you are dealing with hundreds of frames — trying to muscle through that much propolis and wax at room temperature with just a hive tool will destroy your shoulders.

However, propolis and beeswax react to temperature very differently. Beeswax melts beautifully at around 145°F. Propolis, on the other hand, doesn't really melt; it just turns into a sticky, tar-like resin that smears and embeds itself deeper into the wood grain if it gets too hot.

Here is how to tackle the two different batches to maximize speed and minimize damage.

Batch 1: Frames WITH Comb

Because you need to preserve the drawn comb, you can't use broad heat. If the ambient temperature gets much above 115°F, that comb will start to sag and collapse.

  • The Spot-Heat Method: Grab a standard heat gun (like you'd find at Harbor Freight or Home Depot) and set it to low. Keep it moving continuously over the wooden lugs and frame edges where the propolis is thickest. You just want to soften it to the consistency of warm putty so your scraper glides through it. If it starts smoking or bubbling, it's too hot and will just smear.
  • The Cold-Snap Alternative: Counter-intuitively, if a frame is heavy on propolis rather than wax, cold is actually your best friend. Below 50°F, propolis becomes extremely brittle. If you can chill the frames, hitting the propolis with a hive tool will cause it to shatter and flake off cleanly in large chunks without disturbing the comb at all.

Batch 2: Frames WITHOUT Comb (Fully Empty)

Since you don't have to protect any comb here, you can use bulk-heating methods to process dozens of frames an hour.

If these are purely wooden frames (no plastic foundation that could warp), a boiling wash is the gold standard for commercial-scale cleaning. It melts the wax and sanitizes the wood in one go.

If your empty frames have plastic foundation: Do not boil them, as the plastic will permanently warp. Instead, use a DIY steam box. You can build one by piping a cheap wallpaper steamer into an insulated cooler or a wooden box holding the frames. Steam hovers around 212°F, which is hot enough to melt the wax off but gentle enough to keep the plastic intact.
